Natron was used as a desiccant in mummification.
Chemically speaking, this was not lye—which some
modern translations of the word borrowed by the
Greeks and used in Herodotus would have us think—but
a mixture of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate,
together with smaller amounts of sodium chloride and
sodium sulfate, such as was collected by the ancient
Egyptians, mainly on the shores of Wadi el Natrun Lake.
The desiccating effect comes mainly from the crystal-
lized sodium carbonate, to which up to 10% water can
bind without appearing wet. Dehydration could be has-
tened by repeatedly replacing the layers of salt; wood
shavings and linen also supported the process.
After dehydration the body was treated with oint-
ments and resins, sometimes also bitumen. An Egypt-
ian word for “bitumen” was not encountered until the
New Kingdom, but the substance was probably already
known through trade relations with Mesopotamia.
There, it was employed to seal structures against water,
a use the Egyptians noticed and adapted for the pur-
pose of embalming corpses. The relatively late appear-
ance (during the Twentieth Dynasty) of an Egyptian
word for bitumen is matched by archaeological finds.
Analysis of mummies shows the first evidence of bitu-
men in the 9th
century BC (Twenty-Second Dynasty); at
that time it was extracted from natural deposits at
Gebel Zeit (Mons Petrolius) and Abu Durba on the
shores of the Gulf of Suez. In the Greco-Roman period
mummies were also treated with bitumen from the
Dead Sea, which is confirmed not only by analysis, but
by Greek writings. Diodorus Siculus (19.9) mentions the
bitumen of the Dead Sea thus: “The barbarians who
enjoy this source of income take the asphalt to Egypt
and sell it for the embalming of the dead; for unless this
is mixed with the other aromatic ingredients, the
preservation of the bodies cannot be permanent.”6
Posidonios similarly remarks in Strabo (16.2): “The
Egyptians use the asphalt for the embalming of their
dead.”7
Like resin and beeswax, the black-brown sub-
stance softened when heated and was used alone or in
combination with other salve ingredients—there is evi-
dence of blending with animal and vegetable oils. Due
to its liquid-repellant properties, bitumen protected
natron-dried bodies from rehydration and subsequent
decomposition.
Beeswax had a similar effect and was used in mum-
mification from the Middle Kingdom. Beeswax was
not mentioned as an embalming agent in medieval or
early modern texts, but in Egyptian embalming texts
embalms … In Egypt, indeed, the corpse, duly dried, is
actually placed at table—I have seen it done.”4
And
Saint Anthony, an Egyptian monk, was afraid he might
not receive the burial due to a pious Christian, accord-
ing to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (c. 298–373): “if
you have any care for me and are mindful of me as of a
father, suffer no one to take my body into Egypt, lest
haply they place me in the houses.”5
The End of Mummification
With the Edict of Theodosius in 392 AD, all “heathen”
cults were prohibited. The practice of mummification,
however, did not fall under the ban, since Coptic Chris-
tians continued occasionally to preserve the bodies of
especially venerated persons by the use of salt (with-
out, however, evisceration), then storing and taking
care of them (fig. 14). In Christianity, and related cul-
tures, the corpse as a companion of the living has never
become obsolete, as exemplified by Lenin’s mummy
(whose brain was removed for “scientific” investiga-
tion) and the Capuchin catacombs of Palermo,; as well
as the highly complex Christian cult of relics.
In Egypt, meanwhile, the expansion of Islam in 641
AD put an abrupt end to the religious importance of the
human corpse. According to Muslim rite, if a person dies
in the morning he is buried on the same day, otherwise
burial is on the next day. The body—unpreserved, but
washed and wrapped in white cloth—is given to the
earth of Europe, which destroys, or to the sand of the
desert, which still desiccates; respect for the peace of
the deceased is so great that almost any type of orna-
ment or maintenance for the grave is dispensed with, at
least in the case of ordinary mortals.
Appendix: The Most Important
Embalming Agents
Evidence for the agents used in embalming is found in
ancient texts as well as in the material remaining on
mummies and vessels. Analyzing the text sources, such
as from the above-quoted embalming ritual, the ritual
book for the embalming of the Apis bulls, the accounts
from embalming workshops, and the inscriptions from
vessels found in embalming caches, is problematic,
since the ingredients that are named cannot all be iden-
tified with certainty. Only the substances natron,
asphalt, wax, pitch, and myrrh can be safely translated
from their historic meaning.
Certain visible features are typical in mummies of the
Greco-Roman period. First, a refinement of bandaging
techniques was noted (fig. 13). Plaster masks on mum-
mies, mainly from Hermopolis in Middle Egypt, have
been preserved. A distinctive feature that originated in
Egypt during Roman domination (1st
–3rd
centuries AD)
are the so-called portrait mummies, a large number of
which have been found in the necropolises of the
Faiyum Oasis, Antinopolis, and Akhmim. The mummies
were carefully wrapped and their faces are overlaid with
a thin wooden board bearing a portrait of the face of
the deceased painted in encaustic or tempera tech-
nique (figs. 12, 13). The oldest known mummies of this
type come from the reign of the emperor Tiberius
(14–37 AD), the most recent from the 4th
century AD.
The main motive for the introduction of portraits into
the cult of the dead is considered to be the ever-
increasing desire for overt self-portrayal. The deceased
was no longer idealized, but personalized, although he
continued to identify himself with Osiris. Members of
the Roman elite living in Egypt were able to adopt
Egyptian concepts of the afterlife, as proven by images
of funerary art.
There is also a visible change to burial practices.
Sometimes, apparently, years could pass between
death and burial, during which time the mummified
person would remain in the house of his or her surviv-
ing family. The Greek-writing satirist Lucian of
Samosata (c. 120–after 180 AD), who spent several
years in Egypt, described it (De luctu 21): “the Egyptian

status: some of the bodies are natural mummies, while
others have been preserved through human interven-
tion. In total, 94% of these bodies had their brains
removed transnasally; in contrast to the Kharga mum-
mies, however, no embalming liquids had been poured
into the skull. In some of the deceased, the inner organs
were removed through an incision in the left side of the
body or through the rectum, and the body cavities were
filled with embalming matter and resin-soaked balls of
linen. In addition, hot resin had been applied to the
skin—in some cases, this was the only action taken.
There is no evidence that natron had been used to dry
out the corpse.
It is also known from tombs in the Nile Valley that the
methods used often varied. Evisceration was encoun-
tered less in mummies from the Greco-Roman period,
and the use of natron seems to have ceased completely.
All the more conspicuous is the generous use of
embalming agents, which were applied in the body’s
cavities as well as on its surface. In those cases where
the brain had been removed, this was done either in the
traditional way, through the ethmoid bone (lamina
cribrosa) and the nasal cavity, or in a simpler way,
through the large hole at the bottom of the skull (fora-
men magnum).

Greeks for several plant species which are not explicitly
differentiated, namely, for instance, cedar species, such
as Cedrus libani A. Rich., and also species of juniper,
such as Juniperus oxycedrus L., the question arose as
to whether it was cedar resin or oil of juniper (juniper
species do not yield resin, but instead an essential oil)
that was used as an embalming agent. Analysis speaks
convincingly in favor of cedar, however; it is important
to note that traces of Aleppo pine resin have also been
found in mummies dating back as far as the Twenty-
Third Dynasty, as has pistachio resin from Pistacia
lentiscus L.
Among the embalming agents mentioned by
Herodotus and Diodorus was a substance that, so far,
has not been found through analysis: cinnamon. The fact
that it was named as a scent, plus the lack of any sur-
viving traces of it, indicate that cinnamon was not used
as a solid substance, but rather as a scented oil, whose
delicate components have long since evaporated. Cin-
namon—the cassia of which Herodotus spoke, is now
thought to be “China” cinnamon, while the cinnamo-
mum mentioned by Diodorus is “Ceylon” cinnamon. It
was apparently a very unusual ingredient, originating as
it did in faraway regions. There is, at present, no archae-
ological evidence for its importation into Egypt.
Myrrh also had to be imported, and was also counted
among the most precious of ingredients. Today, the
source plant of myrrh for pharmaceutical uses is con-
sidered to be Commiphora molmol (Engl.), but the resin
from other species of Commiphora (family Burser-
aceae) is also referred to as myrrh. This liquid gum resin,
which seeps out of cracks in the tree bark and hardens
on contact with air, gives off a faint, aromatic odor and
has a lingering bitter taste. In the countries where it is
collected it is separated into different grades of quality,
according to its composition, so that imported resin
may consist of a mixture of resin coming from different
source plants. The genus Commiphora comprises over
two hundred species and grows from the Red Sea to
South Africa, and in India. Just as we can hardly deter-
mine the origin of individual resins today, so must we
also accept that the term “myrrh resin” in antiquity has
a very wide-ranging meaning.
it appeared exactly in those places where bitumen
was not named.
Resins were already applied to linen in 4000 BC,
although the antiseptic properties were effective only
when they were in direct contact with the skin. The
remains of resin in mummies were mainly from conifers,
in particular the Aleppo pine (Pinus halepensis Mill.).
Since Egypt was poor in resin-rich tree species, the
embalming agent had to be imported. Starting in the
Eighteenth Dynasty, resin from cedars (Cedrus atlantica
(Endl.) Manetti) was used in mummification. Depending
on the particular type of resin available from traders at
the time, whether resinous wood or lumps of dried
resin, various techniques were needed to prepare the
embalming substance. A viscous, spreadable prepara-
tion was obtained by warming the resin, but heating it
a high temperature under airtight conditions created
pitch. Some texts actually refer to it as a “hot drug”.
Shrouds from the Roman period also feature the jackal-
headed Anubis, the god of the dead responsible for
embalming, in his role as preparer of ointments, cook-
ing the mummification substance on a stove (fig. 15).
Resin was prepared in large amounts, particularly dur-
ing the Roman era. The chemical transformation
processes induced by high temperatures in the wood
tar samples secured by archaeologists can be followed
analytically through their typical ingredients. The anti-
bacterial and antifungal properties of wood tars have
long been known, but a more recent discovery is that
some of the components they contain, principally gua-
iacol and other phenols, have such potent preservative
qualities that an alkaline bone enzyme found in Egypt-
ian mummies is still immunologically and enzymatically
active, even today.
Both Herodotus and Diodorus mention “kedros” as
an embalming agent. Pliny (XXIV, [21] 52), writing about
kedros, says that it was the name for liquid pitch in
Syria, and that it in Europe it is prepared from the Arolla
pine. He described a method of extracting pitch from
wood which is rich in resin. For a long time it was
debated as to exactly which resin kedros referred; as a
rule, the kedros of Herodotus and Diodorus is translated
as “cedar resin”. Since kedros was a word used by the

Summary
In the Ancient and New World there was a custom to preserve the corpse in a natural and
artificial way. Since Paleolithic man believed in an afterlife and even in Mesoamerica and
the Andes cultures, care and ceremony were practiced to the burial of the dead in an ances-
tral cult. Mortuary rituals were developed in Pre-dynastic Egypt (4500-3100 BC) but appar-
ently they had begun before in America, c. 5000 BC.
Mummies served for assisting the soul to survive and for preventing the dead from frighten-
ing the livings. Incas arrived at a point of perfection in these practices after other Andean
cultures but we should not forget their older predecessors, the Chinchorro culture on the arid
coast of the Atacama Desert. Different steps in the technique can be distinguished in both
worlds: natural desiccation covered by animal skins, methods to protect the body skin and
flesh removal, replacement with clay; black, red or mud-coated corpses, evisceration, body
cavity treatment, cleansing and anointing the interior, brain removal, mummified bodies,
corpses covered with natron, before being washed and bandaged or wrapped.
It will be necessary to carefully check dates, techniques and periods in the two zones to estab-
lish exactly the evolution of the methods applied.

Introduction
The Ancient and New World are full of examples of burial customs,
preserving the dead in a natural or artificial form. Although mummified
human remains have been found in almost all continents, especially in six
principal regions, few people introduced this technique responding to re-
ligious purposes, ancestral cult or a belief in the dead powers.1
In the New
World, we can mention the Andean cultures in the Pre-Hispanic America,
Aluet people near Alaska,2
in the North Pacific Ocean,3
including Torres
Strait Islander groups of the coastal areas of north-east Australia,4
and in
the Ancient World the Egyptians in Africa and certain Buddhist priests of
Japan in Asia5
. Mummies have been classified as accidental, (as a result of
natural circumstances, such as heat, cold or chemical soil composition), in-

Agriculture and cemeteries in Egypt
In the North, people migrations to the Nile began in the first Neolithic
(c. 8000 BC) but around 5000 BC Neolithic settlements appeared all over
Egypt. The Northern Merimde culture came about 5000 to 4200 BC, pro-

A new cycle began in 4000
BC, Omari age corresponding to Archaic Period; Buto Maadi cemeteries
appeared at that time. They were not only herders and hunters but they also
cultivated the land.
In the South, Upper Egypt, Badarian small groups of 40 to 100 people,
gathered there from 4400 to 4000 BC, grew wheat and barley and created an
irrigation system. Their practice of wrapping the dead body in animal skins
spread during the Middle and Late Pre-dynastic periods (4500-3100 BC).
At the same time in Northern Fayum A, Calcholite followed the Neolithic
Tasian culture considered Stone Age. Amratian culture or Naqada I, very

Preserving the corps of dead
Is the case of agriculture in America the same as mummification?
Mummies may have served as a means of assisting the soul to survive and
preventing the deceased from frightening the livings. A more commonly ac-
cepted theory is that there was an ancestor cult, delaying the final burial.
Some evidence demonstrates that they travelled with the groups and took
the place of honor during major rituals. The surprising perfection of Incan
technique was achieved after other Andean cultures including their old-
er predecessors, the Chinchorro culture, on the arid coast of the Atacama
Desert between 7000-1500 BC. Their mortuary practices were based on
skills they attained as subsistence hunters and fishermen.

Mummy chronologie and beliefs in America
The cultural diversity of prehispanic America is unified regarding beliefs
about the afterlife and the funeral ritual to become ancestors in a cyclical
life.
Both the Mayan and Mesoamerican civilizations showed great inter-
est in death. They believed that cosmos had three major planes: the Earth,
the Heaven above, celestial paradise of heroic kings and warriors, and the
Underworld Xibalba, translated ‘Place of Fear or Phantoms’. Structured in 9
levels below, reached by caves, cenotes and tunnels, it was dominated by the
aged skeletal Maya god of death and putrefaction Ah Puch, meaning ‘flatu-
lent one’ (fig. 4). Mesoamerican abundant funerary imaginary, recalled now
on the Day of the Dead, was depicted in their artwork: skeletons, skulls, hu-
man carved bones, circular spots on the skin, closed dead eyes, open mouths,
owls and bats, night and darkness, water and lilies.
The skeletal remains, covered with cinnabar or red ochre, an iron or fer-
rum oxide like blood color, symbolized life and rebirth, and had the virtue to
stop putrefaction. It was an expensive material like jade which was used to
give vitality and associated with life because of its green color. A jade bead
in the mouth of corpses, wrapped in cotton mantles and buried with maize
gruel, signified the life spirit and served as money in the afterlife. Only the

Significant advance was reached in the New Kingdom (1570-1070 BC):
mummification had many steps and the process took 70 days. During this
embalming period, extensive rituals were carried out in Per-Nefer, the House

Conclusions
In conclusion the New World was more advanced in the process of mum-
mification than the Old World because:
Undoubtedly Chinchorro natural mummies (7000 BC), painted in
ochre, under environmental conditions from Pacific coast cemeteries, take
precedence over Egyptian natural ones (3500 BC), placed in desert cemeter-
ies. Here this process finished soon, being corpses separated from the en-
closing sand. Both wrapped the burial in animal skins without evidence of
internal modifications.
Chinchorro, the first people in the World to practice artificial mummi-
fication (5000 BC), applied complex internal and external treatments and
Figure 37 - Encaustic portrait of

Death in ancient Egypt, pl. 31)

technique variations. Meanwhile, Egyptian artificial interventions were re-
stricted to linen wrappings (3100-2613 B C) without evisceration.
In Chinchorro culture the mummification was applied to all individu-
als c. 5500 BC but fetuses, neonates, lactating women and children were the

in gold and coffins inlaid with semi-precious stones but later the technique

Black Chinchorro mummies (5050-2500 BC) were completely dismem-
bered, stripping flesh, skin and tissues. The brain, removed by cutting the
skull in half, was dried and tied back together. Almost at the same time
(4000-3200 BC) defleshing and dismembered corpses without head were also
found in Predynastic Egypt, without reassembling later. Only in one case
the brain was removed from the skull base but since 1500 BC, the common
technique involved brain extraction through the nostrils with a metal chisel.
Another Chinchorro characteristic, after the evisceration, was the des-
iccation by heat, the abdominal cavity treated with natural materials, grass
and vegetable or animal fibers, and the body shaped and reinforced with clay.
Instead, in Egypt, around 2613-2498 BC dehydration was rapidly made with
dry natron or simple sand and cavities were packed with resin-soaked linens.
Oils were applied to restore skin elasticity and later in the Eleventh Dynasty
(2060-1991), an oleo-resin enema dissolved viscera.
The Chinchorro task concluded plastering the reassembled bodies with
a white ash paste, modeling genitalia and placing a clay mask over the face
with a short black human hair wig. In Egypt, from 2613 to 2498 BC, modeled
face was sometimes painted with black hair, green eyes and red mouth and
the male sex organs, shaped in cloth, were put in place. Later (2181-2040 BC)
face masks were often made in cartonnage but around 1070-945 BC a doll-
like appearance was created with artificial eyes.
The resulted Chinchorro mummy statue, completely covered in clay, was
wrapped in reeds, and left to dry out for 30-40 days. In Egypt, around 1570-
1070 BC, the embalming sophisticated technique took about 70 days, remov-
ing the brain and saving the nails, but two more economical processes were
carried out in fewer days.
Chinchorro reached a peak in 3000 BC, applying internal and external
treatment to the whole body. In Egypt, the peak was in 1070-945 BC, using

Red Chinchorro technique (2500-2000 BC) evolved practicing many
incisions in the trunk, arms and legs to eviscerate and dry the body cavity
while the head, always cut to remove the brain, was covered with an open eye
clay mask and a wig of 60 cm. long human hair tassels. In Egypt (1570- 1070)
BC), viscera were removed by an incision in the flank, and lungs and other
parts by cutting the diaphragm; except for the heart, ‘the seat of the mind”.
Chinchorro used black manganese or red ochre (5050-2000) to paint
corpses. In Egypt (1570- 1070 BC), resin applications gave dark appearance;
the head was painted in red, black or yellow. By Persian and Greco-Roman
periods, black resin like bitumen was used to consolidate damaged bodies.

Differences
Limbs and spine were strengthened with sticks in Chinchorro culture
to reinforce bodies and in a final style (3000-1300 BC), mud-coat mummies
molded on clay were cemented into their graves, the soil evolution acting as
cementing agent.
Chinchorro soft tissues, just removed, were buried in the westlands or
the ocean while the dry parts were placed in the desert.

In Egypt (2613- 2498 BC), the use of an alabaster box or any container
to embalmed viscera, particularly the liver, intestines, lungs and stomach,
for the royalty, was later replaced (2498- 2181 BC) by canopic jars for lower
classes. But in the Twenty-First Dynasty (1070-945 BC) they were returned
into the body cavity after being dried out in natron and cleaned with spiced
palm wine.
Onion skins or whole bulbs were placed over the eyes or into the ears,
mouth, feet or body cavity, perhaps to stimulate the dead to breathe in the
Sokaris’ Festival.
Animal mummification was very common in Egypt.
Certainly, we can say that the New World mummification arose inde-
pendently and prior to its development in the Old World. However, some
particular methods were used for both cultures with a gap of time, but Egypt
perfected this art due to the advances in its medical science. Finally, both
civilizations abandoned these complex practices, perhaps because they were
expensive, took a long time or were deprived of their religious support.
Sažetak
U starom i novom svijetu postojao je običaj da se tijelo očuva na prirodan i na umjetan na-
čin. Od paleolitika čovjek vjeruje u zagrobni život te čak u srednjoameričkim i andskim kul-
turama,se pokop mrtvih prakticirao uz pažnju i svečanost kroz kult predaka. Pogrebni rituali
razvijeni su u preddinastičkom Egiptu (4500–3100 pr. Kr.) Pogrebni su postupci razvijeni, ali
su se očito počeli i prije, u Americi oko 5000 godina pr. Kr.
Mumije su služile kao oslonac duši za opstanak i za sprečavanje zastrašivanja mrtvih od
strane živućih. Inke su stigle do točke savršenstva u tim postupcima nakon drugih andskih
kultura, ali ne smijemo zaboraviti njihove starije prethodnike, Chinchorro kulturu na suš-
noj obali pustinje Atakama. Različiti stupnjevi u tehnici mogu se razlikovati u oba svijeta:
prirodno sušenje i pokrivanje životinjskom kožom, metode zaštitite tijela; uklanjanje kože i
mesa, zamjena s glinom; u crno, crveno ili u blato obloženi leševi, vađenje utrobe, tretiranje
tjelesnih šupljina, čišćenje i premazivanje unutrašnjosti, uklanjanje mozga, mumificirana
tijela, leševi prekriveni natronom (prirodnom sodom), prije pranja i umatanja u zavoje ili
zamatanja.
Potrebno će biti da pažljivo provjeriti datume, tehnike i razdoblja u obje zone kako bi se pre-
cizno utvrdila evolucija primjenjivanih metoda.
